text:
Psychological First Aid: The First Five Minutes

Anything that could let someone hurt themselves in the next five minutes takes priority, so get the car keys out of reach and turn the stove off, and move them away from roads and balconies, or pools of water for that matter. Letting them move around is fine, and pacing can help, but keep them from taking more of any substance. If they want to go confront somebody, that can wait. And if they want to leave, have someone go with them. Put any weapons away and keep the person away from crowds and strangers. If they want to post their big revelation about the universe, or message an ex, take the phone.

They're feeling overwhelmed, so dim the lights, and clear out the extra people around them.

Then remind them where they are and what's happening, since a trip can make them lose track of it:

You're in [place]. It's [date/time]. You took [substance, if known], and its effects will peak and then change.

Give the Session a Beginning and an End

For planned altered-state work, think through the beginning, middle, and end before starting.

When you have a choice:

Rest and timing: don't begin already depleted. When possible, begin earlier in the day so there is still time for the experience, food, ordinary contact, and sleep afterward.
Physical safety: know the substance and approximate dose, review combinations and medical concerns, prepare the room, and decide in advance what requires outside help.
Intention without a script: know what you are open to exploring without demanding a particular revelation, memory, emotional arc, or spiritual result.
Low-directivity support: the sitter protects safety and offers choices.
Closure: stop adding stimulation, return to the room and date, eat and hydrate when safe, write down the basic facts, and let the body understand that the session has ended.
Integration time: leave the rest of the day and, when possible, the next morning free. Sleep and food come before turning the experience into a new life plan.

opens.first_sentence: Psychological First Aid: The First Five Minutes
opens.why_reading: the heading tells someone looking after a person in a bad state that this is what to do now, in the first five minutes, which is their case; the first paragraph opens on the first thing to do

same_point: none: read the section from its heading to the next for the plan, the list of choices and the pointer back to the triage app; its overlaps are in humanize/h22-20261107/RESULTS.md

questions.Q1: PASS: each paragraph opens on its point: the first priority, the room fixes with their reason, what the reminder is for, then the new section's point under its heading
questions.Q2: PASS: every act in the Human section is the helper's own, with its purpose; the new part says what something means or what practice does, in the reader's terms
questions.Q3: PASS: which things exactly: keys, stove, roads, balconies, pools, weapons, the phone; the lights, the extra people; place, date and time, the substance; the named views and acts
questions.Q4: PASS: no terms a reader would not know; spiritual terms are the guide's own, each said in plain words around it
questions.Q5: PASS: each turn has what it turns on: since a trip makes them lose track; what it is not, then what it is; bypassing, then practice
questions.Q6: PASS: dangers, room, what to say, then the next section's point
questions.Q7: PASS: every fact is about the person in front of them, or how to see what is happening to them
questions.Q8: PASS: the new part is one point, under its heading
questions.Q9: PASS: nothing compressed: the reminder's facts one a sentence, as said aloud; the new part's relations said ('just means', 'that's exactly why')

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
